questions.stem: The transit authority builds vehicle telemetry images on a public Debian base layer before any agency code is added. What does that base layer contribute to the vulnerability findings on these images?

It contributes nothing, because a vendor supplied layer sits outside the agency's control
options.misconception: treats vendor supplied base layers as out of scope

options.misconception: assumes a signed package list proves a clean build

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a container running as root carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain what elevated user identity adds to a container compromise
questions.stem: A control-room scheduling service runs its container as user root so that mounted depot volumes are writable. Reviewers note the container also starts with elevated capabilities. What does running as root add to the blast radius of a compromise?

options.text: It widens what an attacker can alter inside the container, including other processes and mounted files
options.misconception: treats elevated privileges as confined to the container

options.text: It lets a compromise change resources outside the container, so the impact escapes the sandbox
It grants nothing extra, since container isolation applies equally whatever the user identity is
options.misconception: assumes container isolation holds for every user identity

options.text: It only affects ownership of newly created files, with no bearing on runtime privileges
options.misconception: believes root only changes file ownership semantics

questions.explanation: Root inside a container strips the guard rails that limit a compromised process. Damage can then reach host resources wherever isolation is thin, so the account choice matters to exposure.
questions.hint: Ask what the compromised process could still change.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Configuration drift between declared and actual
questions.learningObjective: Explain how configuration drift arises and what to check first
questions.stem: The authority's declared configuration for the depot gateway says the diagnostic port listens only on the loopback address, but the running gateway answers on the depot network. Explain how this drift arose and what a reviewer should check first.

answer.exemplar: The declared state and the running state diverged because a change was applied to the live gateway by hand, or an appliance was restored from a backup carrying older settings, and nothing afterwards re-applied the declared configuration. The reviewer should first compare the complete running configuration with the declared one, identify which fields differ and when each last changed, then confirm whether a configuration management tool is actually enforcing the declared state on every rebuild.

questions.explanation: Drift means the running system no longer matches what was declared and approved. The likeliest cause is a manual or restored change that nothing reapplied, so compare running and declared state first.
questions.hint: Compare the running state with the declared state.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A backup that shares the original's failure
questions.learningObjective: Identify the weakness in a recovery copy stored with the original

stimulus.body: The depot backup run copies the nightly fare system database to a mounted volume in the same region as the live system. The volume sits in the same cloud account as the production database, and the continuity plan lists this copy as the recovery copy. Retention keeps fourteen nights of copies, and no restore has ever been rehearsed.

questions.stem: Given the board paper above, what problem should the authority raise about the recorded recovery copy?

options.text: The fourteen night retention may be shorter than the recovery time the authority has committed to deliver
options.misconception: treats retention length as the only durability concern

options.text: The restore has never been rehearsed, so nobody knows whether the copy can be recovered in time
options.misconception: believes untested restores matter more than failure correlation

options.text: The copy shares the region and account of the live system, so the same failure event can destroy both
The copy is written to a mounted volume, so every write reaches the live database as well
options.misconception: assumes a mounted volume writes through to the live system

questions.explanation: A copy stored with the original shares its failure domain, so one regional event removes the live data and the copy together. Retention and rehearsal matter, but neither protects against the shared failure.
questions.hint: Ask which event would destroy both copies.

options.text: It restores the full volume contents and also the identity configuration the platform consumed at run time
options.misconception: believes a snapshot captures identity configuration

options.text: It restores the data blocks and also the network rules that were in force when the snapshot was taken
options.misconception: believes a snapshot captures network rules

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a container running as root carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk and operational cost of moving a container off root
questions.stem: A depot application container is configured to run as root so it can write to a mounted data volume. The platform team wants to move it to a non-root account. Explain what changes in risk and what could break.

answer.exemplar: Running as root means a compromise of the application inherits administrative rights inside the container, so it can alter other processes, write to mounted volumes and use capabilities a restricted account would not hold. Moving to a non-root account removes those rights, which narrows the blast radius of an exploit and removes the need for the broad privileged capabilities that were added to make root work. It can also break the workload, because the application may need write permission on the mount, access to a specific port below 1024, or ownership changes on files created earlier, so mount permissions and file ownership must be corrected before the switch.

questions.explanation: Dropping root narrows what a compromised container can do, so impact shrinks without fixing the underlying flaw. The cost is operational: mounts, ports and file ownership must be granted deliberately.
questions.hint: Ask what privileged access was really needed for.

questions.topic: The review an infrastructure change needs
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an infrastructure change meets the review condition

stimulus.body: Change request CHG-2041 asks to add a new NAT rule to the depot edge firewall so a supplier can reach the telemetry collector in the evening. The request was raised by the depot supervisor on a Friday afternoon, and the board must decide whether it may proceed in the weekend window.

options.misconception: treats a described rule as a reviewed rule

options.text: Approve it with a deadline, because weekend windows leave no time for a review before the next service day
options.misconception: lets schedule pressure override review

options.text: Hold it for a security review of the rule and the supplier access, since the request lacks both
Reject it outright, because any inbound rule from a supplier is forbidden under the transport policy
options.misconception: treats all supplier access as prohibited

questions.explanation: The request describes a rule but shows no security review and no accountable supplier contact, so it has not met the authority's change conditions. Time pressure is a reason to schedule the review, not to skip it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the request meets the change conditions.

options.text: The backup shares a failure domain with the original, so one event can destroy both copies at once
The backup is unencrypted, so anyone with account access can read every fare record it contains
options.misconception: assumes encryption is the missing control here

options.text: The restore was successful, because the data blocks came back and the platform started cleanly
options.misconception: equates a successful start with a clean restore

options.text: The data came back but the surrounding access did not, so a restore would not return a clean environment
The restore failed, because a snapshot that keeps production access cannot be considered a working copy
options.misconception: treats retained access as proof of restore failure

options.text: The test proves nothing, since a quarterly restore of any system cannot show the true recovery time
options.misconception: dismisses all restore testing as uninformative

questions.explanation: The test shows the blocks recovered while the access around them did not, which is exactly the gap a snapshot leaves. Recovery must include replacing credentials and access rules, not just reattaching a volume.
questions.hint: Ask what else came back besides the data.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Who owns patching the operating system
questions.learningObjective: Divide operating system patch responsibility between supplier and authority
questions.stem: The transit authority buys a supported operating system for its depot servers and uses a vendor base layer for its containers. Explain how responsibility for operating system patching should be divided between them.

answer.exemplar: The authority keeps ownership of the estate it operates: it decides the patch window, applies updates to its depot servers, applies them to the container images it builds, and verifies the results. The vendor keeps ownership of the artefacts it produces: it publishes fixes for the operating system and the base layer, states which versions are supported, and discloses flaws when they are confirmed. The division is not a transfer of blame but a split of actions, and the authority cannot discharge its duty by pointing to the vendor's support commitment, because it alone controls when the patch reaches the running system.

questions.explanation: The vendor is responsible for producing fixes and disclosing flaws; the authority is responsible for applying them in its own estate. Splitting it this way keeps each commitment with the party that can actually act on it.
questions.hint: Ask who controls when the patch reaches the system.

options.misconception: misses that a rebuild alone does not fix the app code

options.text: Rebuild the base layer with current upstream packages and rebuild the images, then re-scan
Ask the vendor to confirm that the base layer is clean before any work begins in the pipeline
options.misconception: assumes vendor assurance replaces the agency's own scan

questions.explanation: Five of nine findings sit in the inherited base layer, so patching containers one at a time treats the symptom. Rebuilding the layer from current upstream packages and rebuilding the images removes it at source.
questions.hint: Look at where most findings are located.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a snapshot fixes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a point in time copy from a full working restore
questions.stem: The vehicle telemetry platform takes a nightly volume snapshot and the depot supervisor asks whether that means the platform can be brought back after a corruption event. Explain the difference between a snapshot and a full restore.

answer.exemplar: A snapshot is a point in time copy of the stored blocks on a volume, and it gives a fast way to recover deleted or corrupted data by copying those blocks back. It is not a restore: restoring also means rebuilding a working environment, reapplying configuration, issuing valid credentials and confirming the identity and network rules are correct. The snapshot answers what the data was, while a restore answers whether the whole system can run again, and only the second question tells the authority whether it can actually recover after an incident.

questions.explanation: A snapshot answers what the data looked like at a point in time. Recovery additionally needs a working environment, valid credentials and correct access rules, which the snapshot never captured.
questions.hint: Ask whether the snapshot contains the access rules.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Configuration drift between declared and actual
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a daily baseline push still leaves drift behind
questions.stem: A transit authority runs a configuration management tool that pushes a declared baseline to 30 depot appliances every night. Explain why drift still appears even though the tool runs daily.

answer.exemplar: Drift appears because the tool runs on a schedule rather than continuously, so any change made directly on a device between runs survives until the next push, and any local edit that survives a push that failed or was skipped is never corrected. Drift also appears when the baseline itself is out of date, because the tool then enforces the wrong state faithfully and the device drifts away from the real design rather than from the baseline. Detection therefore needs both a comparison of running state against baseline and a report of push failures, and the authority should alert on the difference between them rather than assume the daily run has closed it.

questions.explanation: A daily push closes the window only briefly, so manual edits and failed pushes both leave drift behind. The tool also enforces a baseline faithfully even when that baseline is itself wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what happens between runs and when a run fails.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a container running as root carries
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a non root design is achieved for a privileged port workload
questions.stem: A depot dispatcher service must bind to a privileged port and the platform team wants to keep the container running as root. Explain why a non-root design is usually achievable and what makes it work.

answer.exemplar: Most non-root failures come from three places: the process expects to bind a port below 1024, the mounted volume is owned by root so the account cannot write to it, and the application was never tested with a user that has no supplementary groups. Each has a straightforward fix that does not require running as root. A privileged port can be mapped to a high port inside the container and published on the low port outside it, the mount can be given group ownership and a group write bit, and the deployment can run with a fixed non-zero user and matching file ownership. The advantage is that a compromise then inherits only that narrow set of rights, so the blast radius stops at the container in most cases.

questions.explanation: Binding a low port, writing to a mount and holding supplementary groups are the usual blockers, and each has a configuration fix. Non-root then removes most of what a compromise would inherit.
questions.hint: List what actually needs privileged access.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Who owns patching the operating system
questions.learningObjective: Set out the options available when vendor fixes stop
questions.stem: The authority's fleet covers both depot servers and container images, and both sit on operating systems that need regular patching. Explain what the authority should do when a vendor stops publishing fixes.

answer.exemplar: When a vendor stops publishing fixes, the authority has to choose deliberately rather than drift. The first step is to establish the exposure the unpatched platform actually carries, including whether the platform is still reachable from the network the authority fears and whether the affected services can be isolated. The second is to identify the realistic options: move to a supported release of the same product, move to a supported alternative, or accept the risk with a recorded decision, compensating controls and an expiry date. The third is to make sure the decision is written down with a named owner, because an unrecorded acceptance is indistinguishable from an oversight when the audit arrives, and because the exposure grows as the unpatched platform stays in service.

questions.explanation: Losing upstream fixes forces a choice between migrating, compensating and accepting the exposure on the record. Leaving it undecided is the option nobody can defend later, so the decision needs an owner and a review date.
questions.hint: Ask which options are available and who decides.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a snapshot fixes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: Explain the distinct purposes of snapshots and off-region copies
questions.stem: The authority stores nightly snapshots and also keeps a weekly off-region copy. Explain what each is for and why the authority should not treat them as interchangeable.

answer.exemplar: The two mechanisms answer different questions. A snapshot is fast and cheap and covers the recent past in fine detail, so it is the right tool for recovering deleted or corrupted data within the retention window and for the quickest return to service after a small mistake. The off-region copy is coarse, slower and more expensive, and its purpose is to survive the failure of a whole region, a cloud account or the supplier itself, which is precisely what an in-region snapshot cannot do. Treating them as interchangeable leads to two classic errors: designing continuity around the snapshot and then discovering during a drill that the region is gone, or paying the cost of off-region copies while still restoring from a snapshot that shares the original's failure domain.

questions.explanation: Snapshots give speed and fine grained recovery inside the retention window. Off-region copies exist to survive the loss of the region itself, so continuity planning depends on the second while routine recovery uses the first.
questions.hint: Ask which failure each one is designed to survive.

questions.topic: Configuration drift between declared and actual
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unmanaged configuration change should be detected
questions.stem: The authority declares a baseline for its 30 depot appliances and pushes it nightly. A supplier changes one appliance by hand to finish a fault repair. Explain what the authority should have in place to notice this.

answer.exemplar: Nothing in a nightly push detects the edit, because the push will overwrite it and leave no trace, and the change is invisible for the rest of the day. Detection therefore has to come from a source that observes the device continuously rather than from the baseline itself. Three elements do that work: a configuration agent that reports its current state and the last change it applied, an out-of-band integrity check that compares a device attribute against a value recorded outside the device, and a change log on the appliance that a collector reads and forwards centrally. The authority also needs an alert when a collected state disagrees with the baseline, because that disagreement is the only signal that distinguishes a legitimate change from an unmanaged one, and an unmanaged change is precisely what the baseline cannot police on its own.

questions.explanation: A nightly push overwrites the edit without evidence, so detection needs continuous observation rather than enforcement. Collect state and change events from each device and alert on disagreement with the baseline.
questions.hint: Ask what observes the device between pushes.

questions.stem: Given the backup review above, what is the strongest finding?

options.text: The copy should use a shorter retention period, since the fare database changes little overnight
options.misconception: focuses on retention when the failure domain is the issue

options.text: The board should require a rehearsal of restoring the copy before the next continuity exercise
options.misconception: recommends rehearsal without addressing correlated failure

options.text: The recovery source shares an account with the live database and has no off-region copy
The break-glass role should be removed, since key access during an incident delays the recovery
options.misconception: treats the key control as the problem to remove

questions.explanation: The encryption is well separated, so the weakness is the shared account and the absence of an off-region copy. Recovery that depends on a copy inside the account that lost the data cannot be relied on.
questions.hint: Ask which account holds the live data and the copy.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a snapshot fixes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: State what a snapshot guarantees and what a diagram leaves unresolved
questions.stem: An architecture diagram marks the fare database as protected by a nightly snapshot. First state what the snapshot guarantees, then state what the diagram leaves unresolved.

options.text: It guarantees data recovery to last night; it leaves recovery time and credentials unresolved
options.misconception: believes recovery time is already settled by the diagram

options.text: It guarantees a full platform restore; it leaves only the storage cost of doing so unresolved
options.misconception: believes a snapshot restores a running platform

options.text: It guarantees data recovery to last night; it leaves the passphrase used to unlock the copy unresolved
options.misconception: confuses data recovery with credential recovery

options.text: It guarantees recovery of stored data to last night; it leaves access, identity and recovery time unresolved

questions.explanation: The diagram establishes a data recovery point but nothing about the environment around it. Identity, access rules and the time to bring the platform back all remain unresolved, so the diagram overstates the protection on offer.
questions.hint: Ask what the diagram does not cover around the data.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An architecture claim its own identity configuration contradicts
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a granted write action against a stated reach boundary
questions.stem: The authority's design says the depot payment service reaches only the settlement database, yet the identity configuration includes a role with a write action on the customer table. How should this be read?

options.text: The enforced configuration contradicts the design, so one of the two must be corrected deliberately
The design is accurate, because a write action is only meaningful if the application exercises it
options.misconception: treats unused permissions as absent permissions

options.text: Both are true, because the design sets a target and the role is an approved exception
options.misconception: accepts an unreconciled contradiction as normal

options.text: The role is harmless, because the customer table contains no data worth protecting
options.misconception: dismisses a write path without looking at the data

questions.explanation: A granted write action is a path whether or not the code currently uses it, so the configuration contradicts the design. The authority must either narrow the role or change the design through the proper route.
questions.hint: Ask whether a granted path counts even when unused.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Who owns patching the operating system
questions.learningObjective: Locate patch duty where a supplier contract does not reach
questions.stem: The authority's depot servers and its container images use two different operating systems, and only the server platform is covered by a vendor support contract. A board member asks who patches the container layer. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The container vendor, because the layer is derived from their operating system distribution
options.misconception: assumes inheritance transfers patch duty to the vendor

options.text: The authority's platform team, because it assembles and ships the image containing that layer
Nobody, because the layer is inherited and requires no local patch procedure
options.misconception: assumes inherited code needs no patching

options.text: The depot server owners, because both platforms come from the same supplier contract
options.misconception: assumes one contract covers unrelated artefacts

questions.explanation: The contract covers the server platform and says nothing about the image the authority assembles. Patching the container layer sits with the team that builds and ships it, using the vendor's fixes as the source of updates.
questions.hint: Ask which artefact the contract actually names.

questions.topic: What the base image contributes to an image finding
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the flaws closed by rebuilding a fleet of images
questions.stem: A rebuild pipeline runs weekly for 4 bus depot services and produces 12 images per service each week, so 48 images in total. Each rebuild closes 5 base layer flaws in every image it produces. How many base layer flaws are closed across the week's 48 images?
questions.explanation: Four services times 12 images gives 48 images in the week. Each rebuild closes 5 flaws per image, and 48 times 5 gives 240 flaws closed across the week's output.
questions.hint: Multiply the images per week by the flaws closed in each.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a container running as root carries
questions.learningObjective: Set out the checks needed before switching a fleet off root
questions.stem: The depot platform team wants every container in the fleet to run as a fixed non-root account. Explain the checks they should run before switching the fleet over.

answer.exemplar: The team should validate each workload rather than assume the switch will hold. For every image they need to know which files the process writes to and whether the account owns them or has group write access, whether the process binds a port below 1024 and could instead publish a high port, whether it relies on supplementary groups or on a specific home directory and environment path, and whether it writes to a root-owned volume that needs a group ownership change. The rollout should also confirm that the image can express the user as a numeric identifier with no shell, that any health check and entrypoint still work without a login shell, and that the workload has been tested in a way that would have exposed a permission failure before the fleet was moved.

questions.explanation: Switching fails on permissions, ports, groups and paths rather than on the image itself. Those four areas need testing per workload, and a controlled rollout beats a fleet wide cutover.
questions.hint: Check files, ports, groups and paths per workload.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The review an infrastructure change needs
questions.learningObjective: Apply the review rule when a request arrives after the board meeting

stimulus.body: The authority's change board reviews infrastructure changes on the first Tuesday of each month. A request to widen the depot firewall arrived on the eighth, nine days after the last board, and the change window opens before the next board. The requester has attached a written risk assessment and the name of a supplier contact, but no security review. The board's standing procedure states that changes affecting network rules require a completed security review before the change window opens.

questions.stem: Given the review calendar above, what should happen to the firewall request?

options.text: It should proceed, because the window opens before the next board meeting and the risk assessment is attached
options.misconception: lets the change window override the review requirement

options.text: It should proceed, because the supplier contact is named and the authority can contact them if needed
options.misconception: treats a named contact as a security review

options.text: It should wait for the next board, because a completed security review is required before the window
It should be rejected, because requests arriving after a board meeting are never admissible
options.misconception: assumes a late request is automatically inadmissible

questions.explanation: The procedure requires a completed security review before the window opens, and the request has none. The window is a constraint that makes a delay necessary, not a reason to waive the review.
questions.hint: Ask what the standing procedure requires before the window.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Configuration drift between declared and actual
questions.learningObjective: Judge three drifted settings and choose the right remedy
questions.stem: The fare gateway's running configuration differs from its declared baseline on three settings. First judge whether the difference is security relevant, then state the correct way to close it.

options.text: It is relevant only for payment traffic, and it closes by restoring the baseline on the payment gateway first
options.misconception: confines drift to one traffic class

options.text: It is never relevant on its own, and it closes by amending the baseline file to match the gateway
options.misconception: assumes the declaration should absorb any difference

options.text: It is always relevant, and it closes by rebuilding every gateway in the estate from the baseline
options.misconception: rebuilds the whole estate over one drifted gateway

options.text: It is relevant where it widens access, and it closes by restoring or formally reviewing the change

questions.explanation: The judgement is whether the difference widens access or weakens a control, and the three settings need separate assessment. Closing it means restoring the declared state or taking the change through review.
questions.hint: Assess each setting before deciding the remedy.
